# Format: the syntax description (`<command>.py`)

This file states the command's argument syntax: the options it accepts, the type of argument each
option takes, and the types of its operands. It is a Python module that defines one variable.
Downstream programs import the module and read that variable; they do not call anything else in it.

## Shape of the file

```python
from caruca.ir.syntax import *

<command>_syntax_spec: list[SyntaxSpecification] = [
    [                      # one syntax (a command may have several alternative syntaxes)
        [ ...option nodes... ],      # position 0
        [ ...positional nodes... ],  # position 1
    ],
]
```

- The file is named `<command>.py` and the variable is named `<command>_syntax_spec`. Both use the
  command's name, so `tee.py` defines `tee_syntax_spec`.
- All constructors come from the module `caruca.ir.syntax`.
- `<command>_syntax_spec` is a list of **syntaxes**. Each syntax is one way the command line can be laid
  out; most commands have exactly one.
- A syntax is a list of **positions**, in order. Each position is a list of **argument nodes** allowed at
  that position. In every sample, position 0 holds the option nodes and position 1 holds the positional
  operands.

## Argument nodes

An argument node is one constructor call. Two kinds exist.

**`Flag(flag, alias=[...])`** — an option that takes no value, such as `-v` or `--verbose`. The first
argument is the option's spelling; `alias` lists other spellings of the same option.

**Value nodes** — anything that carries a value. The constructor name states the kind of value (see the
vocabulary below). Keyword arguments:

| Keyword | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `flag="-m"` | The node is an option that takes a value, written `-m VALUE`. Omit `flag` and the node is a positional operand instead. |
| `alias=["--max-count"]` | Other spellings of the same option. |
| `flag_followed_by_equals=True` | The value is attached with `=`, as in `--interactive=always`. |
| `choices=["never", "once", "always"]` | The allowed values, for `Selection` and `String`. |
| `arity=Arity.<name>` | How many times this node may appear on the command line (see below). |
| `dash_as_stdin=True` | On `Path` only: a lone `-` in this position means standard input. |

`Integer` also accepts `min=` and `max=` (an inclusive value range) and `suffixes=(...)`.
`List` describes a separator-joined list of values and accepts `of=<value node type>` and `separator=","`.

## Arity

`arity` says how many times a node may appear, not how many values it takes. The default is `OPTIONAL`.

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Arity.OPTIONAL`, `Arity.ZERO_OR_ONE` | zero or one time (the default) |
| `Arity.EXACTLY_ONE` | exactly once |
| `Arity.EXACTLY_TWO` | exactly twice |
| `Arity.ZERO_OR_MORE` | any number of times, including none |
| `Arity.AT_LEAST_ONE`, `Arity.ONE_OR_MORE` | one or more times |

## Vocabulary of value nodes

Each name below is a constructor exported by `caruca.ir.syntax`. Names on the same line are the same type
under different names.

| Constructor | Value it stands for |
|---|---|
| `Path` | a file or directory path |
| `Integer`, `Int`, `Number`, `Pid`, `Duration` | an integer |
| `String`, `Other`, `User`, `Format` | free text; `Other` is the catch-all when nothing more specific fits |
| `Selection` | one value out of a fixed set given in `choices` |
| `List` | several values joined by a separator |
| `Regex` | a regular expression |
| `Glob` | a shell wildcard pattern such as `*.txt` |
| `Separator`, `Delimiter` | a delimiter string |
| `Char` | a single character |
| `Range` | a numeric range such as `1-2` or `1,3` |
| `Size` | a size with a unit suffix, such as `1k` or `1m` |
| `Permission` | a file permission such as `u+r` or `0755` |
| `OwnerGroup` | an `owner:group` pair |
| `Group` | a group name |
| `Signal` | a signal name or number |
| `Variable` | an environment variable name |
| `Command` | the name of another command |
| `Hostname` | a host name |
| `Filesystem` | a filesystem type such as `ext4` |
| `Date`, `DateTime` | a date or a date-time |
| `DateFormat` | a `strftime`-style date format |
| `TimeStyle` | a time style name such as `iso` or `full-iso` |
| `Expression` | an arithmetic expression |
| `PrintfFormat`, `SprintfFormat` | a `printf`-style format string |
| `Geometry` | a size or percentage such as `100x100` or `50%` |
| `SecurityContext`, `SecurityRange`, `SecurityRole`, `SecurityType` | SELinux security attributes |

# Format: the behaviour annotation, as PaSh consumes it

PaSh describes a command with three files. Together they let PaSh parse an invocation of the command,
work out which of its arguments are inputs and outputs, and decide whether the invocation's work can be
split across parallel copies. The files live in the `pash_annotations` Python package (the module
paths below are that package's), and the samples under `samples/*/annotation/` are copied from it unchanged.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `<command>.json` | the parser table: the command's flags and options, and the type of each option's argument |
| `InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, marks which operands and option arguments are read, which are written, and whether standard input and standard output are used |
| `ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, lists the ways its work may be split and recombined; when the file is absent, PaSh treats the command as not parallelisable |

`<Command>` is the command's name with its first letter capitalised (`grep` → `Grep`).

## 1. The parser table, `<command>.json`

```json
{
    "flag": [
        ["-c", "--count"],
        ["-D"],
        "-f"
    ],
    "option": [
        ["-e", "PATTERNS"],
        ["--regexp", "PATTERNS"],
        ["-f", "--file", ["FILE", "CONFIG_INPUT"]]
    ]
}
```

- `flag` lists the options that take no argument. Each entry is a list of the spellings of one flag;
  the first spelling is the one the parser reports. A bare string is accepted as a one-spelling entry.
- `option` lists the options that take an argument. Each entry is one or more spellings followed by
  the argument's type name. The type name is free text taken from the manual (`NUM`, `WHEN`, `MODE`),
  except that a file argument is written as a two-element list, `["FILE", <access>]`, where `FILE`,
  `DIR` or `DIRECTORY` marks it as a path and `<access>` is one of the access kinds in section 4.
- Two spellings of the same option may be listed as separate entries (grep's `-e` and `--regexp`) or in
  one entry (`-f`, `--file`).

PaSh's parser reads an invocation left to right: words found in `flag` or `option` are collected, with
an option consuming the following word as its argument; a word of the form `-abc` whose letters are all
flags is split into them; the first word that is none of these starts the operand list.

## 2. The input/output class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.InputOutputInfoGenerator_Interface import InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface


class InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>(InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

The class defines one method, `generate_info`. PaSh constructs the object with the parsed invocation,
calls `generate_info`, and reads the result. Before `generate_info` runs, every operand is already
marked as a streaming input and option arguments are already typed from the parser table; the method
changes what differs for this command and this invocation.

**Inspecting the invocation** (inherited):

| Call | Returns |
|---|---|
| `self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-q", "-c"])` | whether any of the named flags or options is present |
| `self.get_flag_option_list_filtered_with([...])` | the present ones among those named |
| `self.get_operand_list_length()` | the number of operands |
| `self.get_first_operand_name_as_string()` | the first operand's text |
| `self.does_first_operand_start_with(s)`, `self.does_first_operand_contain(s)` | tests on that text |
| `self.cmd_inv.flag_option_list`, `self.cmd_inv.operand_list` | the parsed lists themselves |

**Declaring inputs and outputs** (inherited):

| Call | Effect |
|---|---|
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdin()` | standard input is read even though no operand names it |
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdout()` | standard output is written |
| `self.if_no_operands_given_stdin_implicitly_used()` | the first, only when there are no operands |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_inputs()` | every operand is a file read as a stream (the default) |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_outputs()` | every operand is a file written as a stream |
| `self.all_operands_are_other_inputs()` / `..._other_outputs()` | every operand is a file read, or written, in some non-streaming way |
| `self.all_but_last_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._other_input()` | the last operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.all_but_first_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._streaming_output()` / `..._other_input()` | the first operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.only_last_operand_is_stream_output()` / `..._other_output()` | the last operand alone is an output |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_string()` | the first operand is not a file but a value, such as a pattern |
| `self.set_all_operands_as_config_arg_type_string()` | no operand is a file |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_filename_or_std_descriptor()` | the first operand is a file read as configuration rather than as a stream |

## 3. The parallelizability class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator_Interface import ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface


class ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>(ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

Again one method, `generate_info`, with the same inspection calls as above. It appends zero or more
**parallelizers** to a list. A parallelizer is a splitter, a mapper and an aggregator: how the input is
divided, what runs on each part, and how the parts' outputs are recombined. Appending nothing means the
invocation is not parallelised.

**Splitters:** `indiv_files` (each input file is its own part), `consec_chunks` (the input is cut into
consecutive pieces), `round_robin` (lines are dealt out to parts in turn).

**Mappers:** by default the same command runs on each part (`seq`). A custom mapper is named with
`make_mapper_spec_custom(name, is_implemented=...)` from
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.MapperSpec`.

**Aggregators:** `conc` (concatenate the parts' outputs in order; the default), `adj_lines_merge`
(merge the boundary lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_seq` (run the command itself over the boundary
lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_func` (a named function over the boundary lines), and custom
2-ary or n-ary functions. The `make_aggregator_spec_*` constructors live in
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.AggregatorSpec`; the ones that take
a function name also take `is_implemented`, and a name beginning `PLACEHOLDER:` marks a function PaSh
does not yet provide.

**Appending a parallelizer**, in two forms:

- The inherited one-call shortcuts, named `append_to_parallelizer_list_<splitter>_seq_<aggregator>`
  with splitter in `if`, `cc`, `rr` and aggregator in `conc`, `adjm`, `adjs`, `adjf`; the `adjf` ones
  take `(string_repr_func, is_implemented)`. Examples: `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_cc_seq_conc()`,
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_rr_seq_adjs()`.
- Building one explicitly with `make_parallelizer_consec_chunks(...)`,
  `make_parallelizer_round_robin(...)` or `make_parallelizer_indiv_files(...)` from
  `pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.Parallelizer`, each taking
  optional `mapper_spec`, `aggregator_spec` and `info_splitter_mapper` (an
  `AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper` value: `NO_ADD_INPUT`, `LINE_NUM_OFFSET`, `BYTE_OFFSET`,
  `LINE_NUM_AND_BYTE_OFFSET`, for mappers that need to know where their part began), then
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer)`.

`self.set_commutative()` records that the parts' outputs may be recombined in any order.

## 4. Access kinds

Used in the parser table's file-argument entries and behind the input/output calls above:

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `STREAM_INPUT` | a file read as the data stream the command processes |
| `CONFIG_INPUT` | a file read for configuration, such as a pattern file |
| `CONTAINER_FOR_INPUT` | a file that lists the real input files |
| `EXCLUDES_FROM_INPUT` | a file that lists what to leave out |
| `OTHER_INPUT` | read in some other way |
| `STREAM_OUTPUT` | a file written as the output stream |
| `OTHER_OUTPUT` | written, created or removed in some other way |
======

# Format: the behaviour annotation, as PaSh consumes it

PaSh describes a command with three files. Together they let PaSh parse an invocation of the command,
work out which of its arguments are inputs and outputs, and decide whether the invocation's work can be
split across parallel copies. The files live in the `pash_annotations` Python package (the module
paths below are that package's), and the samples under `samples/*/annotation/` are copied from it unchanged.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `<command>.json` | the parser table: the command's flags and options, and the type of each option's argument |
| `InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, marks which operands and option arguments are read, which are written, and whether standard input and standard output are used |
| `ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, lists the ways its work may be split and recombined; when the file is absent, PaSh treats the command as not parallelisable |

`<Command>` is the command's name with its first letter capitalised (`grep` → `Grep`).

## 1. The parser table, `<command>.json`

```json
{
    "flag": [
        ["-c", "--count"],
        ["-D"],
        "-f"
    ],
    "option": [
        ["-e", "PATTERNS"],
        ["--regexp", "PATTERNS"],
        ["-f", "--file", ["FILE", "CONFIG_INPUT"]]
    ]
}
```

- `flag` lists the options that take no argument. Each entry is a list of the spellings of one flag;
  the first spelling is the one the parser reports. A bare string is accepted as a one-spelling entry.
- `option` lists the options that take an argument. Each entry is one or more spellings followed by
  the argument's type name. The type name is free text taken from the manual (`NUM`, `WHEN`, `MODE`),
  except that a file argument is written as a two-element list, `["FILE", <access>]`, where `FILE`,
  `DIR` or `DIRECTORY` marks it as a path and `<access>` is one of the access kinds in section 4.
- Two spellings of the same option may be listed as separate entries (grep's `-e` and `--regexp`) or in
  one entry (`-f`, `--file`).

PaSh's parser reads an invocation left to right: words found in `flag` or `option` are collected, with
an option consuming the following word as its argument; a word of the form `-abc` whose letters are all
flags is split into them; the first word that is none of these starts the operand list.

## 2. The input/output class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.InputOutputInfoGenerator_Interface import InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface


class InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>(InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

The class defines one method, `generate_info`. PaSh constructs the object with the parsed invocation,
calls `generate_info`, and reads the result. Before `generate_info` runs, every operand is already
marked as a streaming input and option arguments are already typed from the parser table; the method
changes what differs for this command and this invocation.

**Inspecting the invocation** (inherited):

| Call | Returns |
|---|---|
| `self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-q", "-c"])` | whether any of the named flags or options is present |
| `self.get_flag_option_list_filtered_with([...])` | the present ones among those named |
| `self.get_operand_list_length()` | the number of operands |
| `self.get_first_operand_name_as_string()` | the first operand's text |
| `self.does_first_operand_start_with(s)`, `self.does_first_operand_contain(s)` | tests on that text |
| `self.cmd_inv.flag_option_list`, `self.cmd_inv.operand_list` | the parsed lists themselves |

**Declaring inputs and outputs** (inherited):

| Call | Effect |
|---|---|
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdin()` | standard input is read even though no operand names it |
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdout()` | standard output is written |
| `self.if_no_operands_given_stdin_implicitly_used()` | the first, only when there are no operands |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_inputs()` | every operand is a file read as a stream (the default) |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_outputs()` | every operand is a file written as a stream |
| `self.all_operands_are_other_inputs()` / `..._other_outputs()` | every operand is a file read, or written, in some non-streaming way |
| `self.all_but_last_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._other_input()` | the last operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.all_but_first_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._streaming_output()` / `..._other_input()` | the first operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.only_last_operand_is_stream_output()` / `..._other_output()` | the last operand alone is an output |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_string()` | the first operand is not a file but a value, such as a pattern |
| `self.set_all_operands_as_config_arg_type_string()` | no operand is a file |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_filename_or_std_descriptor()` | the first operand is a file read as configuration rather than as a stream |

## 3. The parallelizability class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator_Interface import ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface


class ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>(ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

Again one method, `generate_info`, with the same inspection calls as above. It appends zero or more
**parallelizers** to a list. A parallelizer is a splitter, a mapper and an aggregator: how the input is
divided, what runs on each part, and how the parts' outputs are recombined. Appending nothing means the
invocation is not parallelised.

**Splitters:** `indiv_files` (each input file is its own part), `consec_chunks` (the input is cut into
consecutive pieces), `round_robin` (lines are dealt out to parts in turn).

**Mappers:** by default the same command runs on each part (`seq`). A custom mapper is named with
`make_mapper_spec_custom(name, is_implemented=...)` from
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.MapperSpec`.

**Aggregators:** `conc` (concatenate the parts' outputs in order; the default), `adj_lines_merge`
(merge the boundary lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_seq` (run the command itself over the boundary
lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_func` (a named function over the boundary lines), and custom
2-ary or n-ary functions. The `make_aggregator_spec_*` constructors live in
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.AggregatorSpec`; the ones that take
a function name also take `is_implemented`, and a name beginning `PLACEHOLDER:` marks a function PaSh
does not yet provide.

**Appending a parallelizer**, in two forms:

- The inherited one-call shortcuts, named `append_to_parallelizer_list_<splitter>_seq_<aggregator>`
  with splitter in `if`, `cc`, `rr` and aggregator in `conc`, `adjm`, `adjs`, `adjf`; the `adjf` ones
  take `(string_repr_func, is_implemented)`. Examples: `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_cc_seq_conc()`,
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_rr_seq_adjs()`.
- Building one explicitly with `make_parallelizer_consec_chunks(...)`,
  `make_parallelizer_round_robin(...)` or `make_parallelizer_indiv_files(...)` from
  `pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.Parallelizer`, each taking
  optional `mapper_spec`, `aggregator_spec` and `info_splitter_mapper` (an
  `AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper` value: `NO_ADD_INPUT`, `LINE_NUM_OFFSET`, `BYTE_OFFSET`,
  `LINE_NUM_AND_BYTE_OFFSET`, for mappers that need to know where their part began), then
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer)`.

`self.set_commutative()` records that the parts' outputs may be recombined in any order.

## 4. Access kinds

Used in the parser table's file-argument entries and behind the input/output calls above:

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `STREAM_INPUT` | a file read as the data stream the command processes |
| `CONFIG_INPUT` | a file read for configuration, such as a pattern file |
| `CONTAINER_FOR_INPUT` | a file that lists the real input files |
| `EXCLUDES_FROM_INPUT` | a file that lists what to leave out |
| `OTHER_INPUT` | read in some other way |
| `STREAM_OUTPUT` | a file written as the output stream |
| `OTHER_OUTPUT` | written, created or removed in some other way |

XARGS(1)		    General Commands Manual		      XARGS(1)

NAME
       xargs - build and execute command lines from standard input

SYNOPSIS
       xargs [options] [command [initial-arguments]]

DESCRIPTION
       This manual page documents the GNU version of xargs.  xargs reads items
       from  the  standard  input, delimited by blanks (which can be protected
       with double or single quotes or a backslash) or newlines, and  executes
       the  command (default is echo) one or more times with any initial-argu‐
       ments followed by items read from standard input.  Blank lines  on  the
       standard input are ignored.

       The  command line for command is built up until it reaches a system-de‐
       fined limit (unless the -n and -L options  are  used).	The  specified
       command	will  be invoked as many times as necessary to use up the list
       of input items.	In general, there will be many	fewer  invocations  of
       command	than  there  were items in the input.  This will normally have
       significant performance benefits.  Some commands can usefully  be  exe‐
       cuted in parallel too; see the -P option.

       Because	Unix  filenames	 can contain blanks and newlines, this default
       behaviour is often problematic; filenames containing blanks and/or new‐
       lines are incorrectly processed by xargs.  In these  situations	it  is
       better to use the -0 option, which prevents such problems.   When using
       this option you will need to ensure that the program which produces the
       input  for  xargs  also	uses a null character as a separator.  If that
       program is GNU find for example, the -print0 option does this for you.

       If any invocation of the command exits with a status of 255, xargs will
       stop immediately without reading any further input.  An	error  message
       is issued on stderr when this happens.

OPTIONS
       -0, --null
	      Input  items  are	 terminated  by a null character instead of by
	      whitespace, and the quotes and backslash are not special	(every
	      character is taken literally).  Disables the end of file string,
	      which  is	 treated  like	any other argument.  Useful when input
	      items might contain white space, quote  marks,  or  backslashes.
	      The  GNU	find  -print0  option produces input suitable for this
	      mode.

       -a file, --arg-file=file
	      Read items from file instead of standard input.  If you use this
	      option, stdin remains unchanged when commands are	 run.	Other‐
	      wise, stdin is redirected from /dev/null.

       --delimiter=delim, -d delim
	      Input  items  are	 terminated  by	 the specified character.  The
	      specified delimiter may be a single character, a C-style charac‐
	      ter escape such as \n, or an octal or hexadecimal	 escape	 code.
	      Octal  and  hexadecimal  escape  codes are understood as for the
	      printf command.	Multibyte characters are not supported.	  When
	      processing  the  input,  quotes  and  backslash are not special;
	      every character in the input is taken literally.	The -d	option
	      disables any end-of-file string, which is treated like any other
	      argument.	  You  can  use this option when the input consists of
	      simply newline-separated items, although	it  is	almost	always
	      better to design your program to use --null where this is possi‐
	      ble.

       -E eof-str
	      Set  the	end  of	 file  string  to eof-str.  If the end of file
	      string occurs as a line of input, the rest of the input  is  ig‐
	      nored.   If  neither -E nor -e is used, no end of file string is
	      used.

       -e[eof-str], --eof[=eof-str]
	      This option is a synonym for the -E option.  Use -E instead, be‐
	      cause it is POSIX compliant while this option is not.   If  eof-
	      str  is  omitted, there is no end of file string.	 If neither -E
	      nor -e is used, no end of file string is used.

       -I replace-str
	      Replace occurrences of replace-str in the initial-arguments with
	      names read from standard input.  Also, unquoted  blanks  do  not
	      terminate	 input	items;	instead	 the  separator is the newline
	      character.  Implies -x and -L 1.

       -i[replace-str], --replace[=replace-str]
	      This option is a synonym for  -Ireplace-str  if  replace-str  is
	      specified.   If  the replace-str argument is missing, the effect
	      is the same as -I{}.  This option is deprecated; use -I instead.

       -L max-lines
	      Use at most max-lines nonblank input  lines  per	command	 line.
	      Trailing blanks cause an input line to be logically continued on
	      the next input line.  Implies -x.

       -l[max-lines], --max-lines[=max-lines]
	      Synonym for the -L option.  Unlike -L, the max-lines argument is
	      optional.	  If  max-lines	 is not specified, it defaults to one.
	      The -l option is deprecated since the POSIX  standard  specifies
	      -L instead.

       -n max-args, --max-args=max-args
	      Use  at  most  max-args  arguments per command line.  Fewer than
	      max-args arguments will be used if the size (see the -s  option)
	      is  exceeded, unless the -x option is given, in which case xargs
	      will exit.

       -P max-procs, --max-procs=max-procs
	      Run up to max-procs processes at a time; the default is  1.   If
	      max-procs	 is 0, xargs will run as many processes as possible at
	      a time.  Use the -n option or the -L option with	-P;  otherwise
	      chances  are  that  only	one exec will be done.	While xargs is
	      running, you can send its process a SIGUSR1 signal  to  increase
	      the  number  of  commands to run simultaneously, or a SIGUSR2 to
	      decrease the number.  You cannot increase it above an  implemen‐
	      tation-defined  limit  (which is shown with --show-limits).  You
	      cannot decrease it below 1.  xargs  never	 terminates  its  com‐
	      mands; when asked to decrease, it merely waits for more than one
	      existing command to terminate before starting another.

	      Please  note  that  it is up to the called processes to properly
	      manage parallel access to shared	resources.   For  example,  if
	      more  than one of them tries to print to stdout, the output will
	      be produced in an indeterminate order (and very likely mixed up)
	      unless the processes collaborate in some way  to	prevent	 this.
	      Using  some  kind	 of  locking scheme is one way to prevent such
	      problems.	 In general, using a locking scheme will  help	ensure
	      correct  output  but  reduce  performance.  If you don't want to
	      tolerate the performance difference,  simply  arrange  for  each
	      process to produce a separate output file (or otherwise use sep‐
	      arate resources).

       -o, --open-tty
	      Reopen  stdin  as /dev/tty in the child process before executing
	      the command.  This is useful if you want xargs to run an	inter‐
	      active application.

       -p, --interactive
	      Prompt  the user about whether to run each command line and read
	      a line from the terminal.	 Only run the command line if the  re‐
	      sponse starts with `y' or `Y'.  Implies -t.

       --process-slot-var=name
	      Set the environment variable name to a unique value in each run‐
	      ning  child process.  Values are reused once child processes ex‐
	      it.  This can be used in a rudimentary load distribution scheme,
	      for example.

       -r, --no-run-if-empty
	      If the standard input does not contain any nonblanks, do not run
	      the command.  Normally, the command is run once even if there is
	      no input.	 This option is a GNU extension.

       -s max-chars, --max-chars=max-chars
	      Use at most max-chars characters per command line, including the
	      command and initial-arguments and the terminating nulls  at  the
	      ends of the argument strings.  The largest allowed value is sys‐
	      tem-dependent,  and  is  calculated as the argument length limit
	      for exec, less the size of your environment, less 2048 bytes  of
	      headroom.	  If this value is more than 128KiB, 128Kib is used as
	      the default value; otherwise, the default value is the  maximum.
	      1KiB  is 1024 bytes.  xargs automatically adapts to tighter con‐
	      straints.

       --show-limits
	      Display the limits on the command-line length which are  imposed
	      by the operating system, xargs' choice of buffer size and the -s
	      option.	Pipe  the  input  from	/dev/null (and perhaps specify
	      --no-run-if-empty) if you don't want xargs to do anything.

       -t, --verbose
	      Print the command line on the standard error output before  exe‐
	      cuting it.

       -x, --exit
	      Exit if the size (see the -s option) is exceeded.

       --help Print a summary of the options to xargs and exit.

       --version
	      Print the version number of xargs and exit.

       The  options  --max-lines  (-L,	-l), --replace (-I, -i) and --max-args
       (-n) are mutually exclusive. If some of them are specified at the  same
       time,  then  xargs  will generally use the option specified last on the
       command line, i.e., it will reset the value  of	the  offending	option
       (given  before) to its default value.  Additionally, xargs will issue a
       warning diagnostic on stderr.  The exception to this rule is  that  the
       special	max-args value 1 ('-n1') is ignored after the --replace option
       and its aliases -I and -i, because it would not actually conflict.

EXAMPLES
       find /tmp -name core -type f -print | xargs /bin/rm -f

       Find files named core in or below the directory /tmp and	 delete	 them.
       Note  that  this	 will work incorrectly if there are any filenames con‐
       taining newlines or spaces.

       find /tmp -name core -type f -print0 | xargs -0 /bin/rm -f

       Find files named core in or below the directory /tmp and	 delete	 them,
       processing  filenames  in  such a way that file or directory names con‐
       taining spaces or newlines are correctly handled.

       find /tmp -depth -name core -type f -delete

       Find files named core in or below the directory /tmp and	 delete	 them,
       but more efficiently than in the previous example (because we avoid the
       need  to use fork(2) and exec(2) to launch rm and we don't need the ex‐
       tra xargs process).

       cut -d: -f1 < /etc/passwd | sort | xargs echo

       Generates a compact listing of all the users on the system.

EXIT STATUS
       xargs exits with the following status:

	      0	     if it succeeds

	      123    if any invocation of the command exited with status 1-125

	      124    if the command exited with status 255

	      125    if the command is killed by a signal

	      126    if the command cannot be run

	      127    if the command is not found

	      1	     if some other error occurred.

       Exit codes greater than 128 are used by the shell to  indicate  that  a
       program died due to a fatal signal.

STANDARDS CONFORMANCE
       As of GNU xargs version 4.2.9, the default behaviour of xargs is not to
       have  a	logical end-of-file marker.  POSIX (IEEE Std 1003.1, 2004 Edi‐
       tion) allows this.

       The -l and -i options appear in the 1997 version of the POSIX standard,
       but do not appear in the 2004 version of the standard.	Therefore  you
       should use -L and -I instead, respectively.

       The -o option is an extension to the POSIX standard for better compati‐
       bility with BSD.

       The  POSIX  standard allows implementations to have a limit on the size
       of arguments to the exec functions.  This limit could be as low as 4096
       bytes including the  size  of  the  environment.	  For  scripts	to  be
       portable,  they must not rely on a larger value.	 However, I know of no
       implementation whose actual limit is that small.	 The --show-limits op‐
       tion can be used to discover the actual limits in force on the  current
       system.

BUGS
       It  is not possible for xargs to be used securely, since there will al‐
       ways be a time gap between the production of the list  of  input	 files
       and  their  use in the commands that xargs issues.  If other users have
       access to the system, they can manipulate the  filesystem  during  this
       time  window to force the action of the commands xargs runs to apply to
       files that you didn't intend.  For a more detailed discussion  of  this
       and  related  problems, please refer to the ``Security Considerations''
       chapter in the findutils Texinfo documentation.	The -execdir option of
       find can often be used as a more secure alternative.

       When you use the -I option, each line read from the input  is  buffered
       internally.    This means that there is an upper limit on the length of
       input line that xargs will accept when used with	 the  -I  option.   To
       work  around this limitation, you can use the -s option to increase the
       amount of buffer space that xargs uses, and you can also use  an	 extra
       invocation  of  xargs to ensure that very long lines do not occur.  For

       somecommand | xargs -s 50000 echo | xargs -I '{}' -s 100000 rm '{}'

       cause  it  doesn't  use	the -i option.	The second invocation of xargs
       does have such a limit, but we have ensured that it never encounters  a

NAME
       xargs - build and execute command lines from standard input

SYNOPSIS
       xargs [options] [command [initial-arguments]]

DESCRIPTION
       This manual page documents the GNU version of xargs.  xargs reads items
       from  the  standard  input, delimited by blanks (which can be protected
       with double or single quotes or a backslash) or newlines, and  executes
       the  command (default is echo) one or more times with any initial-argu‐
       ments followed by items read from standard input.  Blank lines  on  the
       standard input are ignored.

       The  command line for command is built up until it reaches a system-de‐
       fined limit (unless the -n and -L options  are  used).	The  specified
       command	will  be invoked as many times as necessary to use up the list
       of input items.	In general, there will be many	fewer  invocations  of
       command	than  there  were items in the input.  This will normally have
       significant performance benefits.  Some commands can usefully  be  exe‐
       cuted in parallel too; see the -P option.

       Because	Unix  filenames	 can contain blanks and newlines, this default
       behaviour is often problematic; filenames containing blanks and/or new‐
       lines are incorrectly processed by xargs.  In these  situations	it  is
       better to use the -0 option, which prevents such problems.   When using
       this option you will need to ensure that the program which produces the
       input  for  xargs  also	uses a null character as a separator.  If that
       program is GNU find for example, the -print0 option does this for you.

       If any invocation of the command exits with a status of 255, xargs will
       stop immediately without reading any further input.  An	error  message
       is issued on stderr when this happens.

	      character is taken literally).  Disables the end of file string,
	      which  is	 treated  like	any other argument.  Useful when input
	      items might contain white space, quote  marks,  or  backslashes.
	      The  GNU	find  -print0  option produces input suitable for this
	      mode.

	      Read items from file instead of standard input.  If you use this
	      option, stdin remains unchanged when commands are	 run.	Other‐
	      wise, stdin is redirected from /dev/null.

	      specified delimiter may be a single character, a C-style charac‐
	      ter escape such as \n, or an octal or hexadecimal	 escape	 code.

	      printf command.	Multibyte characters are not supported.	  When

	      every character in the input is taken literally.	The -d	option
	      disables any end-of-file string, which is treated like any other
	      argument.	  You  can  use this option when the input consists of
	      simply newline-separated items, although	it  is	almost	always
	      better to design your program to use --null where this is possi‐

	      string occurs as a line of input, the rest of the input  is  ig‐

## What I produced

**`output/xargs.py`** — one syntax: 21 option nodes covering every spelling in `xargs --help` (an automated diff of help text vs. spec came back empty in both directions), plus two operands: `Command()` for COMMAND and `String(arity=ZERO_OR_MORE)` for INITIAL-ARGS. - `-a/--arg-file` is a `Path` with `dash_as_stdin=True` (`-a -` reads stdin).
- `-d/--delimiter` is a `Delimiter`; the binary rejects multi-character values but accepts escapes like `\n`.
